## What to Eat in Lisbon: 12 Must-Try Portuguese Dishes
No trip to Lisbon is complete without tasting a warm pastel de nata. These small custard tarts are made with creamy egg yolk custard nestled in a crisp, flaky puff pastry shell. You’ll often find them dusted with cinnamon or powdered sugar and best enjoyed warm, straight from the oven. The original recipe comes from the Belém district’s famous Pastéis de Belém bakery, but countless cafés around the city offer equally delicious versions of this beloved treat. ## 2. ## Lisbon Food Guide: Best Dishes & Restaurants (2026)
Lisbon’s food scene has a logic to it. The city eats well because it always had to — Atlantic fish on the doorstep, olive oil and wine from the interior, spices routed through the port from half the world. That history is still on the plate. Century-old tascas serve bacalhau from the same recipes their grandmothers used. Seafood arrives fresh from the Atlantic every morning. Pastéis de nata come out of the oven around the clock. And a younger generation of chefs is now pulling all of it apart [...] The Portuguese claim 365 ways to cook bacalhau — one for every day of the year. This salt-preserved cod has been the backbone of Portuguese cooking since the Age of Discovery, when it sustained sailors on long Atlantic voyages. ## Portuguese Food: 25 Dishes to Try in Portugal (With Recipes)
The pastel de nata refers to egg tarts invented in the 17th century by monks at the Jeronimos Monastery in Lisbon. At the time, egg whites were used to starch clothing which left the monks with a surplus of egg yolks to be used in cakes and pastries. One of the pastries they invented was the pastel de nata. [...] ## PORTUGUESE SEAFOOD DISHES ### 9. Bacalhau Together with pastel de nata, bacalhau is perhaps the most well-known dish in Portuguese cuisine. It’s a Portuguese national dish and far and away the most commonly eaten type of fish in Portugal. [...] You can have pastel de nata anywhere in Portugal, but the most famous Portuguese custard tarts are from Pasteis de Belem in Lisbon. It’s home to the original Jeronimos Monastery recipe for these delicious egg tarts, a Portuguese recipe that’s remains unchanged even after 180 years.

plan.title: 3 Days in Lisbon: What to See and Eat
plan.description: A three-day Lisbon plan covering Alfama and the castle, Belém, and a day trip to Sintra. Plus the pastries, cod and sardines you should taste along the way.

beats.narration: Imagine a yellow tram rattling up a steep hill, a warm custard tart in your hand, and the Atlantic glittering below. Lisbon packs all of that into just three days.
beats.chapter: Why Lisbon works in three days

beats.narration: Three days cover the essentials: Alfama and the castle, then Belém, then a day trip to Sintra. Each day works on its own, so you can adjust the order.
Stay somewhere central. Chiado, Baixa and Alfama let you reach many major sights on foot, which saves time and tired legs.
Start high, at Castelo de São Jorge. Afterwards, wander down into Alfama. Narrow streets, colorful buildings and tiny squares are all right next to the castle.
Then ride Tram 28. It runs seven kilometers from Martim Moniz to Campo de Ourique, passing Graça, Alfama, Baixa, Chiado and Estrela.

props.title: Tram 28
props.caption: About 45 to 50 minutes end to end

beats.narration: A ticket on board costs €3.30 in 2026. Ride before nine in the morning or after seven in the evening, when it is calmer.
Day two heads west to Belém. Climb the sixteenth-century Belém Tower, a UNESCO site, then visit the nearby Jerónimos Monastery.
Now the reward. Monks at the Jerónimos Monastery invented the pastel de nata. Pastéis de Belém still uses the original recipe, unchanged after 180 years.

Try bacalhau, salt-preserved cod. The Portuguese claim 365 ways to cook it, one for every day of the year.

beats.narration: Start with bacalhau à Brás, shredded cod with eggs, onions and matchstick potatoes. Then bacalhau com natas, baked in cream like a gratin.
Also taste grilled sardines, bifana sandwiches, octopus à lagareiro and arroz de marisco. A food tour is a fun way to try them all.
On day three, take the easy day trip to Sintra. It is one of the highlights of visiting the area, so plan at least one full day.
Back in the city, end with a slow evening and a small glass of ginjinha in a quiet square.
So: castle and Alfama, Belém and tarts, then Sintra. Eat cod, sardines and custard tarts, and Lisbon will stay with you long after three days.
